content: Abortion during the second trimester of pregnancy constitutes approximately 10-15% of all abortions performed globally. In most developed countries, dilation and evacuation (D&E) is the preferred method for second-trimester abortion. Cervical preparation is strongly recommended for dilation and curettage (D&C) after 12 weeks of gestation and is considered standard practice for D&E procedures performed beyond 14 weeks of gestation. Various methods, including prostaglandins, osmotic dilators, and Foley balloon catheters, have been utilized and studied for cervical preparation prior to second-trimester D&E. However, there is no consensus on which method is superior in terms of safety, procedure duration, the need for additional dilation, procedural success, or acceptability to both patients and providers. The introduction of osmotic dilators has enhanced the safety of second-trimester D&E procedures. However, it remains unclear whether one type of osmotic dilator is superior to another or whether combining osmotic dilation with prostaglandins offers advantages over using osmotic dilators or prostaglandins alone. This review specifically evaluates the effectiveness of different cervical preparation methods for second-trimester surgical abortion. It examines factors such as procedure time, the degree of cervical dilation achieved, the need for additional dilation, complication rates, procedural success, patient pain levels, and satisfaction among both patients and providers. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared various cervical preparation methods, including osmotic, mechanical, antiprogesterone, prostaglandin, or other medical agents, for second-trimester surgical abortion between 14 and 24 weeks of gestation. Data were extracted by two authors and verified by a third, with statistical analyses performed to calculate mean differences and Peto Odds Ratios. The findings indicate that osmotic dilators are superior to prostaglandins in achieving cervical dilation throughout the second trimester and in reducing procedure time during the early second trimester. However, adding prostaglandins to osmotic dilators did not significantly enhance cervical dilation, except after 19 weeks of gestation, and had no effect on procedure time. The combination of mifepristone and misoprostol improved cervical dilation but was associated with longer procedure times and higher rates of pre-procedural expulsions. Two-day cervical preparation resulted in greater cervical dilation compared to one-day preparation, but it did not affect procedure time. Importantly, there were no significant differences in serious complication rates or the ability to complete the procedure across the various preparation methods. In conclusion, cervical preparation using osmotic dilators and/or misoprostol before second-trimester D&E is both safe and effective. Osmotic dilators provide superior cervical dilation compared to prostaglandins alone or in combination with prostaglandins, but this does not translate into differences in procedure time or complication rates. For pregnancies under 19 weeks of gestation, there appears to be no clear clinical advantage to two-day cervical preparation over one-day preparation. The combination of mifepristone and misoprostol is associated with high rates of pre-procedural expulsions and does not seem to be a practical method for cervical preparation before second-trimester D&E. Same-day procedures are considered safe and feasible during the early second trimester, but further research is needed to evaluate their safety and efficacy in the later second trimester.
